title: Act V, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: Defeated, Brutus asks Clitus, Dardanius and Volumnius in turn to help him die; all refuse. He tells them Caesar's ghost appeared to him again at Philippi. Strato holds his sword and Brutus runs on it, saying 'Caesar, now be still: I kill'd not thee with half so good a will.' Antony and Octavius arrive. Antony calls Brutus 'the noblest Roman of them all,' the only conspirator who acted for the common good, not envy. Octavius orders an honorable burial and ends the play.

context.history: Plutarch reports that Brutus died by his own hand after Philippi, assisted by Strato, in 42 BC. Octavius later became Augustus, Rome's first emperor, ending the republic Brutus tried to save.

significance: The play closes with Antony's tribute, which reframes Brutus. Irony: the act meant to preserve the republic helped bring about the empire. Note: this scene depicts suicide; use safe messaging and offer support.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act V, Scene V,” how does Shakespeare show the death of Brutus? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act V, Scene V, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the death of Brutus? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act V, Scene V develops the idea of the death of Brutus. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act V, Scene V (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of the death of Brutus. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act V, Scene V suggests about the death of Brutus. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act V, Scene V to complicate the reader's understanding of the death of Brutus. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act V, Scene V within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the death of Brutus responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act V, Scene V alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the death of Brutus follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act V, Scene V and its treatment of the death of Brutus. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act V, Scene V as evidence for a larger claim about the death of Brutus in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act V, Scene V as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the death of Brutus. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Can a person be noble and still be wrong? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: This scene shows a death by suicide. Support is available if this is hard to read. If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are tarrying, slaying, bondage, entertain, elements. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Fly, fly, my lord; there is no tarrying here.” In this sentence it means: staying; lingering. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Julius Caesar would have known. Plutarch reports that Brutus died by his own hand after Philippi, assisted by Strato, in 42 BC. Octavius later became Augustus, Rome's first emperor, ending the republic Brutus tried to save. Why does this scene matter? The play closes with Antony's tribute, which reframes Brutus. Irony: the act meant to preserve the republic helped bring about the empire. Note: this scene depicts suicide; use safe messaging and offer support. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script:
Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “This was the noblest Roman of them all:
All the conspirators save only he
Did that they did in envy of great Caesar;
He only, in a general honest thought
And common good to all, made one of them.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the death of Brutus? I circle “elements”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find characterization, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to power, ambition and tyranny? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
